narr: Let's explore the key events and figures in the history of Uzbekistan during the 20th century.
We'll start by examining significant historical events, then look at important statistics that shaped the nation.

events.text: War: 1,433,230 participants; 280 Heroes of the Soviet Union
Uzbek becomes the state language; demonstrations in Fergana, etc.
I. Karimov elected president (the first among the republics in the USSR)
Declaration of Independence (12 articles, 2nd session of the 12th convocation)
GKChP; Gorbachev isolated; Karimov's visit to India interrupted
Proclamation of independence; the Law «On the Foundations of State Independence»
Independence referendum; the first nationwide elections of the President

narr: The history of Uzbekistan in the 20th century was marked by significant political and social events.
Between 1937 and 1953, approximately 100,000 people were repressed, with 13,000 executed.
During World War II, from 1941 to 1945, Uzbekistan contributed 1.4 million participants to the war effort, with 280 individuals receiving the title of Hero of the Soviet Union.
The period of 1943 to 1944 saw mass deportations, including approximately 110,000 Meskhetians and 151,424 Crimean Tatars.
In the 1980s, Uzbekistan experienced the «Cotton Affair» from 1983 to 1985, resulting in over 25,000 arrests.
April 1985 marked the beginning of Gorbachev's perestroika policy.
By 1989, Uzbek was declared the state language, and demonstrations occurred in Fergana and other regions.
In March 1990, Islam Karimov was elected president, making him the first republican president in the USSR.
June 18-20, 1990 saw the Declaration of Independence with 12 articles.
The August 19, 1991 GKChP coup attempt led to Gorbachev's isolation and interrupted Karimov's visit to India.
On August 31, 1991, Uzbekistan proclaimed independence and passed the Law «On the Foundations of State Independence».
September 1 was declared Independence Day.
On December 29, 1991, an independence referendum was held with over 98% support, along with the first nationwide presidential elections.
Now let's examine some key statistics that provide insight into Uzbekistan's historical development.
These figures cover various aspects including participation in war, repressions, educational achievements, and economic data.

data.heading: War Statistics
rows: war participants from Uzbekistan (>40% of the able-bodied)
killed / missing / did not return / disabled
awarded / Heroes of the Soviet Union

narr: During World War II, Uzbekistan contributed significantly to the war effort.
Over 1.4 million people participated, representing more than 40% of the able-bodied population.
The casualties were substantial, with 263,000 killed, 132,670 missing, 395,795 not returning, and 60,452 disabled.
Approximately 120,000 were awarded various honors, with 280 receiving the title of Hero of the Soviet Union, 75 of whom were ethnic Uzbeks.

data.heading: Repression Statistics
rows: convicted by the NKVD troikas of 1937–1939 / shot
dekulakized farms / repressed dekhkans / exiled families

narr: The Soviet period was marked by significant repressions in Uzbekistan.
Between 1937 and 1939, 41,000 were convicted by NKVD troikas, with 6,920 executed.
From 1937 to 1953, approximately 100,000 were repressed, with 13,000 shot.
The «Cotton Affair» in the 1980s led to over 25,000 arrests.
Additionally, 40,000 farms were dekulakized, 6,920 dekhkans were repressed, and 5,500 families were exiled.
Uzbekistan experienced significant educational advancement during the Soviet period.
Literacy rates increased dramatically from 11% in 1928 to 68% by 1939.
By 1940, there were 5,504 schools with 1,368,800 pupils, compared to 82,300 pupils in 1924.
The number of specialists with diplomas reached 55,300 by 1941.
The region also experienced significant population movements, with 74,500 Koreans, 110,000 Meskhetian Turks, and 151,424 Crimean Tatars affected by deportations.

data.heading: Economic Statistics
rows: minerals per year / value over the last 15 years of the USSR

narr: Uzbekistan possesses significant natural resources.
In the 1980s, the country produced over 250 billion cubic meters of gas annually and more than 50 tons of gold.
The value of minerals extracted was $5.5 billion per year, totaling $75 billion over the last 15 years of the USSR.
By 1985, there were 1,549 industrial enterprises operating in Uzbekistan.

data.heading: Infrastructure and Governance Statistics
rows: share of Uzbeks in the governing bodies 1924–1928–1930

narr: Uzbekistan has developed extensive infrastructure, particularly in irrigation.
The country has 197,000 kilometers of irrigation canals and 23 reservoirs with a total capacity of 10 billion cubic meters.
The representation of Uzbeks in governing bodies increased from 23% in 1924 to 32.3% in 1928 and reached 75% by 1930.
Timur's empire at its peak covered an area of 10 million square kilometers.
